question: What exactly is a 'specimen' when you are caring for a patient?

options.A: A sterile instrument used during a surgical procedure
options.B: A prescribed medication dose given during a shift
options.C: A sample of tissue or body fluid taken for laboratory examination
options.D: A written record of the patient daily vital signs

explanation: A specimen is simply any biological sample (like blood or urine) collected from a patient to help run lab tests. You'll be collecting these all the time! [learn more](GNS112_U6_T4#GNS112_U6_T4_h1)

question: Why must you, as the nurse, use great care when collecting laboratory specimens?

options.A: It decreases the overall cost of running hospital diagnostic equipment
options.B: It ensures the lab results reflect the true condition of the patient
options.C: It shortens the length of time the patient stays in the hospital
options.D: It removes the need for doctors to physically examine the patient

explanation: Spot-on! Good collection habits prevent errors and contamination, meaning the doctor gets accurate results to treat your patient properly. [learn more](GNS112_U6_T4#GNS112_U6_T4_h1)

question: What is the single best way to stop germs from spreading when handling specimens?

options.A: Changing the patient room air filters daily
options.B: Wearing two pairs of sterile gloves at all times
options.C: Spraying the examination table with bleach
options.D: Proper hand hygiene before and after the procedure

explanation: Simple handwashing remains your greatest superpower in infection control. Wash your hands religiously! [learn more](GNS112_U6_T4#GNS112_U6_T4_h2)

question: What should you do immediately after using a needle to draw blood?

options.A: Carefully scoop the needle cap back on using one hand to prevent injury
options.B: Place the needle on a clean tray until the end of the shift
options.C: Break the needle tip off with forceps before throwing it in the bin
options.D: Drop the unrecapped needle directly into a puncture-resistant sharps container

explanation: Never recap needles! Dropping them straight into the sharps box right beside you is the safest way to avoid accidental needle-pricks. [learn more](GNS112_U6_T4#GNS112_U6_T4_h2)

question: Why do we prefer a 'clean-catch midstream' urine sample when checking for a urinary tract infection?

options.A: It contains a higher concentration of red blood cells
options.B: It requires less total volume than a random urine sample
options.C: It eliminates the need for any patient preparation
options.D: It avoids collecting bacteria from around the urethral opening

explanation: By letting the first bit of urine flush away skin germs, the midstream sample gives a true picture of what is actually inside the urinary tract. [learn more](GNS112_U6_T4#GNS112_U6_T4_h3)

question: How do you properly start a 24-hour urine collection test for a patient?

options.A: Save all urine produced starting from midnight regardless of when the patient last urinated
options.B: Collect the very first morning urine sample and use that exact time to start the 24-hour clock
options.C: Wait until the patient drinks two liters of water before collecting the first sample
options.D: Have the patient empty their bladder completely, discard that urine, and start the timer

explanation: Always throw away that very first void to empty the bladder completely, then start your 24-hour clock with a clean slate! [learn more](GNS112_U6_T4#GNS112_U6_T4_h3)

question: Which everyday substance must definitely be kept out of a stool sample?
explanation: Urine mixes easily with stool and can ruin lab tests for parasites or blood. Always ask patients to pass urine first! [learn more](GNS112_U6_T4#GNS112_U6_T4_h4)

question: What does a black, tarry stool sample usually tell you about your patient?

options.A: Bleeding in the upper gastrointestinal tract
options.B: Bleeding in the lower rectum or anus
options.C: Severe dehydration and low fluid intake
options.D: A high intake of green leafy vegetables

explanation: As blood travels all the way from the stomach through the gut, digestive juices break it down, turning it dark and tarry by the time it comes out. [learn more](GNS112_U6_T4#GNS112_U6_T4_h4)

question: When is the best time of day to collect a sputum (phlegm) sample?

options.A: Just before the patient goes to sleep at night
options.B: Right after the patient takes a warm shower
options.C: Immediately after a heavy lunch or dinner meal
options.D: Early in the morning before eating or drinking

explanation: Secretions pool in the airways overnight, making early morning the absolute best time to catch a good deep cough sample. [learn more](GNS112_U6_T4#GNS112_U6_T4_h5)

question: How is true sputum different from ordinary saliva?

options.A: Saliva is thick and colored green or yellow due to infection
options.B: Sputum is produced entirely by glands inside the oral cavity
options.C: Saliva contains high amounts of blood and cellular debris
options.D: Sputum comes from deep in the lungs and lower respiratory tract

explanation: Saliva is just mouth fluid, but sputum comes coughing up from the lungs and bronchial tubes, which is what the lab needs to see. [learn more](GNS112_U6_T4#GNS112_U6_T4_h5)

question: If a patient vomits something that looks like coffee grounds, what does that usually mean?

options.A: Partially digested blood from the stomach
options.B: A complete blockage of the large intestine
options.C: The recent consumption of dark roasted coffee
options.D: Excessive production of normal bile fluid

explanation: Classic clinical sign! Stomach acid reacts with bleeding in the upper GI tract, giving old blood that distinct coffee-ground texture. [learn more](GNS112_U6_T4#GNS112_U6_T4_h6)

question: Why might a patient's vomit turn a bright green or yellow color?

options.A: It is a normal sign of eating green vegetables
options.B: It indicates that food was digested properly in the small intestine
options.C: It proves the patient has a severe bacterial lung infection
options.D: It often appears after prolonged vomiting when the stomach is empty

explanation: Once the stomach is completely empty from throwing up, continuous vomiting brings up bright green or yellow bile from the small intestine. [learn more](GNS112_U6_T4#GNS112_U6_T4_h6)

question: At what point should you label a specimen container with the patient details?

options.A: Only after the laboratory technician asks for confirmation
options.B: Immediately at the bedside in the presence of the patient
options.C: After returning to the nursing station at the end of the shift
options.D: Before entering the patient room to save working time

explanation: Always label right at the bedside! Doing it later invites dangerous mix-ups between patients. [learn more](GNS112_U6_T4#GNS112_U6_T4_h7)

question: What is the main danger of leaving a collected lab specimen sitting at room temperature for too long?

options.A: Bacteria can multiply and cells can break down, giving false results
options.B: The label on the container will automatically fade and fall off
options.C: The specimen container will become legally invalid for testing
options.D: Hospital management will issue a fine for delayed paperwork

explanation: Time matters! Leaving samples sitting around lets bacteria multiply or cells decay, which ruins the accuracy of the test. [learn more](GNS112_U6_T4#GNS112_U6_T4_h7)
